label.reasoning: The student must state the expected shape of a distribution (skewed left), i.e., describe a representation of one quantitative variable, not justify a claim from computed results.

The student must design/describe an experiment—random assignment, control group, comparison—which is justifying an appropriate method for ethically gathering data, not merely identifying given information.

The student must interpret correlation/p-value results to evaluate causal claims and justify conclusions in context—assessing meaning of results rather than computing or constructing. That matches 4.D.

The dominant task is designing an experiment—specifying treatment/control, random assignment, blocking justification—i.e., justifying an appropriate method for ethically gathering data, rather than merely identifying given information.
The student is asked only to compute summary statistics (mean and standard deviation) from raw data, not describe, compare, or justify—matching skill 3.B.

The central task is carrying out the chi-square test: computing the statistic, df, and p-value. Though table construction and probabilities appear, the dominant graded work is producing inference-method results.

Most parts ask students to compute probabilities (addition rule, complement, multiplication for independent events); the justification part is secondary. Dominant task is calculating probabilities, matching 3.C.

The dominant task is describing and defending a sampling procedure—using a random digit table correctly and explaining why an SRS avoids bias versus convenience sampling—which is justifying an appropriate method for ethically gathering data, not merely identifying information.

Multiple parts, but the centerpiece task is building the bar graph (with axes, labels, gaps) from computed relative frequencies; description and justification are secondary. Construction dominates the scoring criteria.

Though parts a–b involve computing and describing, the culminating task (part c) requires justifying which measure of center is appropriate based on the computed results—arguing a claim from calculations. 4.B best captures the overall demand.

The item's central performance is building a modified boxplot (part b), with outlier computation supporting it; description in part c is secondary. Constructing a graphical representation is the dominant task.

The dominant tasks are computing expected counts in a hypothetical 1000-person table and calculating a conditional probability; part C's explanation is secondary. This matches calculating expected counts and probabilities.

The bulk of the task is computing marginal/conditional distributions and comparing them to describe the relationship; the comparison of distributions dominates, even though part c asks a conclusion. Primary cognitive task is describing/comparing representations and summary statistics.

Parts a and c ask for computing mean and SD of a random variable; parts b and d interpret. The dominant, prerequisite task across scoring points is calculating summary statistics (expected value, variance, SD), with interpretation secondary—but weight is balanced; calculation drives the item.

Though part a justifies binomial conditions and part b computes a probability, the bulk and culminating task involves computing distribution parameters—mean and SD—for a binomial random variable, matching 3.D.

The bulk of the item asks students to describe and justify design choices—random assignment, blocking, and why it's an experiment—i.e., justifying an appropriate method for ethically gathering data, rather than merely identifying information.

All parts require computing normal probabilities and a percentile cutoff (inverse normal), including a sampling-distribution probability. The dominant task is calculating probabilities/values from a normal model, matching 3.C rather than computing distribution parameters or describing distributions.

Though part (a) and (c) involve calculation, the dominant task across parts is comparing the two distributions' shape, center, and spread in context—describing distributions and comparing them, which is 4.A (compare representations and summary statistics).

Student must identify the sampling method, sources/direction of bias, and describe a better sampling procedure — identifying relevant information about data collection methods rather than computing or interpreting inference. This matches skill 1.B-style design description, but among given options, 2.A fits identifying information to answer the question.
Though parts a and d are computations (4.A-like), the dominant scored task is justifying claims about mutual exclusivity and independence from probability calculations, matching 4.B.
Student designs/carries out a simulation and computes the proportion of successful trials to estimate a probability — estimating a probability, matching 3.C.

Though part a asks to construct a table (3.A), the bulk of the task—E(Y), variance, SD—is computing statistics from a probability distribution, i.e., 3.B calculate summary statistics/probabilities/parameters. But "single best" given hint 3.A... Majority of scoring focuses on calculations.

Multi-part item includes classifying variables, computing a conditional distribution, constructing a segmented bar graph, and comparing. The culminating/most weighted graded task centers on building the representation (3.A), though comparison appears in part d. Part c's construction plus part b's computation of distributions dominate.

The dominant task across parts is computing probabilities—joint, total, and conditional (Bayes)—with the independence check resting on comparing calculated probabilities. That matches calculating probabilities.

Though part a involves computation, the item overall centers on describing/comparing shapes, spreads, and summary statistics of two distributions and reasoning how statistics change—primarily a comparison-of-representations task (4.A).

The task is computing mean/SD, checking conditions, and calculating a Normal-approximation probability — statistical computation, not describing/comparing distributions. Best fit is the "determine/calculate" skill (3.B); given only 4.C listed, but the asked action is calculation of probabilities.

The student constructs a mosaic plot (graphical representation) and reads off a feature of the distribution—producing/describing a representation rather than justifying a claim with statistical reasoning.
Student constructs boxplots and compares center and spread between two distributions in context — describing/comparing representations and summary statistics, i.e., 4.A.

Student constructs a segmented bar graph from relative frequencies and describes/compares the distributions across groups—representation construction and comparison, not justifying a claim with statistical reasoning beyond description.
The primary task is building a dotplot from raw data; description follows but construction dominates the scoring criteria (scale, correct dots). That matches constructing graphical representations.

Student constructs graphical representations and compares center and spread of two distributions in context—describing/comparing representations and summary statistics, not justifying a claim or computing statistics.

Student constructs graphical representations and compares center and spread of two distributions — describing/comparing representations and summary statistics, i.e., 2.B-style graphing plus comparison, best matched by 4.A.

Student constructs boxplots and compares center and spread between two distributions in context — that's describing/comparing representations and summary statistics, skill 4.A.

The student constructs a segmented bar graph from relative frequencies and compares groups—creating/describing a representation, not justifying a claim with evidence-based reasoning. The task is constructing a mosaic plot (a graphical representation) and reading off a feature from it — producing/describing representations of two categorical variables, not justifying a claim with statistical reasoning.

The student constructs a graphical representation (mosaic plot) of two categorical variables and reads off a feature — representing/describing distributions rather than justifying a claim with evidence.

The primary task is constructing a dotplot; most scoring criteria address building the graph correctly (scale, dots). Description of shape is secondary, so 3.A fits best.
Student must justify which measures are appropriate given skew/outliers—reasoning from the distribution's features to support a claim, not computing statistics or merely describing them.
Student must choose and justify appropriate measures of center/spread based on the distribution's skew and outlier—justifying a claim from given results, not computing or merely describing.

The task is constructing a segmented bar graph from relative frequencies and describing/comparing the distributions (whether satisfied proportion increased)—a representation and comparison task, not justifying a claim via inference or calculation-based argument.

The primary task is constructing a dotplot (graphical representation of one quantitative variable), with description secondary. Scoring emphasizes scale and correct dot placement, matching skill 2.A? No—constructing graphs is 2.A? In AP Stats, 2.A is constructing graphs for categorical... Actually the provided list gives 3.A for constructing tabular/graphical representations.

Student must evaluate the observational study design and judge what conclusion is appropriate (association vs. causation) — justifying appropriate inference from the data-collection method, matching 2.B rather than merely identifying information.
Student must explain/justify why blocking is an appropriate design choice for gathering data—evaluating the merit of a data collection method, not merely extracting information.

Student must evaluate the observational (non-randomized, volunteer) design and judge what conclusion the data-collection method ethically/validly supports — justifying an appropriate method/scope of inference rather than extracting given values.
The student must explain/justify why blocking is an appropriate design choice for gathering data—evaluating the benefit of a randomized block design rather than extracting given information.
Student must compute z-scores (relative position) for each score and identify which is larger—this is calculating relative position, skill 3.B, rather than justifying a claim from given results.
The student must compute the standard deviation of a sum of independent random variables—a numerical summary statistic calculation—rather than interpret a result or claim.

Student must reason about how sampling distribution shape/variability behave as n grows—interpreting the meaning of CLT results rather than computing a numeric mean/SD or checking conditions for an inference procedure.

Student must interpret how the sampling distribution's shape and standard error behave as n grows—reasoning about meaning of CLT results rather than computing a value or checking conditions for an inference procedure.

The student must check the large counts (success-failure) condition to decide whether the normal approximation method is appropriate—verifying conditions for the procedure, not computing a parameter or interpreting a result.
The student must choose the correct interpretation of a confidence interval, not use it to justify a claim. That matches interpreting inference-method results.
The student must decide whether the t-interval's normality/random conditions are met, justifying appropriateness by verifying conditions—not selecting among methods or computing results.

The student must check the large-counts condition (expected counts ≥5) and decide how to remedy a violation—verifying conditions to justify the inference method, rather than selecting a test or stating hypotheses.

The student interprets a p-value and states a conclusion in context, including scope of inference (observational study, no causation). That's justifying a claim from a significance test, not calculating—so 4.E/4.B-type skill rather than the listed 3.B. Only 3.B is provided.

Student selects appropriate summary statistics given distribution shape — a conceptual judgment about describing center/spread of a representation, not computing or justifying from calculations. Fits 4.A.
The student must compute a standardized score (relative position) from given mean and SD — a calculation task, matching 3.B.
The student must choose the correct interpretation of a confidence interval, not use it to justify a claim. That is interpreting inference-method results.
Student must compute the new mean (sum increases by 12, divided by 12 values), a calculation of a summary statistic, not describing a distribution or justifying a claim.
Student reads a boxplot and selects the verbal description of shape and outliers—describing a graphical representation rather than justifying a claim with calculations.
Student isn't computing a statistic or justifying from results; they must compare properties of summary statistics (resistance to outliers), which is describing/comparing summary statistics.

Student must identify the correct method for computing the median with an even number of observations—essentially applying the calculation rule for a summary statistic, not describing a distribution or justifying a claim.

Student computes Q3 + 1.5(IQR), a numerical summary statistic calculation used for boxplot outlier identification. Among the two options, this is not constructing a display; it's working with summary statistics, best fitting 4.A.
The student must interpret what a percentile (relative position) means—describing/interpreting a summary statistic rather than computing one or justifying a claim. That matches 4.A.

Student selects the appropriate description of a symmetric distribution's center summary statistics—describing/comparing summary statistics relative to shape, not justifying a claim from computed results.

Student must evaluate sampling methods and select/justify the appropriate way to gather data randomly, avoiding bias — that's justifying an appropriate data collection method, not extracting information.
Student must explain/justify why stratified sampling is an appropriate data-collection method, i.e., justify a sampling method rather than extract information—matching 2.B.

Student must justify/select an appropriate data-collection design (blocking by age before random assignment), i.e., choosing an ethical/appropriate method for gathering data rather than extracting given information.

The question asks the student to identify/classify the study type from the described scenario (no treatment assigned), which is identifying information rather than justifying a data-collection method.

Student must explain/justify why random assignment is appropriate—its role in balancing confounding variables for valid causal inference—rather than extracting given information. That is justifying an appropriate data-collection method.
Student must recognize/identify which listed item could plausibly be a confounding variable — selecting relevant information rather than justifying a data-collection or representation method.
Student must recognize/identify the type of bias present in the described sampling method—identifying information relevant to the problem rather than computing or justifying. Only 2.A is available.
Student must explain/justify why double-blinding is an appropriate design feature for ethically and validly gathering data—justifying a method, not merely extracting information.
Student must recognize/identify the data collection method term (census) from a described scenario—identifying information about how data were gathered, not justifying a method or posing a question.
The student must compute a conditional probability from given counts, which is calculating a probability — matching skill 3.C.
Student must compute a joint probability via the multiplication rule — a numerical probability calculation, matching skill 3.C.
Student must compute a complement probability, a direct numerical probability calculation, matching 3.C.
Student must compute P(A)P(B) and compare to P(A and B) to justify independence—a probability calculation task. Only 3.C is offered, and it fits the computation of probabilities.
The student must compute the mean of a discrete random variable (10×0.2), a summary statistic calculation, not an interpretation of meaning or claim.

Student must select and justify the conclusion (card can't be both suits) using the mutually exclusive reasoning — i.e., justify a claim based on the probability concept/result, matching 4.B, the only listed skill.
The student must compute a probability using the addition rule, which is calculating a probability—matching skill 3.C.

Student must identify/verify the conditions defining a binomial setting—checking whether conditions are met, a justification-of-claim-type conceptual task rather than computing probabilities or parameters.

Student must identify/justify the appropriate counting method for an unordered selection, choosing among permutation/combination — a reasoned claim about method rather than computing a value or distribution parameter.
The student must compute σ/√n, a numerical calculation of a sampling distribution's parameter (standard deviation of x̄), matching skill 3.D rather than interpreting or verifying conditions.

Student must reason about how margin of error changes with sample size—an interval computation/result relationship, not condition checking or method selection. Best fits calculating inference-method results (3.E).

The student must explain/justify why normality holds by checking the large-sample (CLT) condition — verifying a condition that justifies normal-based inference, rather than computing or interpreting a result.

The student must compute the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of p̂ using the formula √(p(1-p)/n) — a calculation of a parameter for a probability distribution, not interpretation or condition checking.
Student compares standard errors (σ/√n) for two sample sizes—essentially computing/evaluating a parameter of the sampling distribution, not checking conditions or interpreting a claim in context.
Student must interpret the described estimator behavior (consistently off the true value) and identify bias—justifying a conclusion about the estimator's property rather than computing a mean or SD.
Student must compare p-value to α and state the decision/conclusion from an inference procedure — interpreting inference-method results (4.F).
Student must compute power = 1 − β, a numerical calculation of a probability, even though the topic is errors. The task performed is calculating a probability.
Student must choose which inference procedure fits the paired design—selecting an appropriate method, not stating hypotheses or checking conditions.
The student must select the correct null and alternative hypotheses for a population proportion, which is precisely identifying hypotheses rather than choosing a method or verifying conditions.
Student must recognize the relationship between sample size and power—components of inference methods—rather than compute or interpret a result.
Student must compute a marginal proportion (30/100) from a two-way table — a numerical summary statistic calculation, not description or justification.

Student selects the correct probability formula (Bayes) rather than computing—but among available skills, this is identifying/applying the appropriate probability expression, best matching 3.C (probability determination).
Student computes a binomial probability P(X=0), a direct probability calculation, not a mean/SD or interpretation.
The task is computing an expected cell count = (row × column)/grand total, matching "calculate/estimate expected counts," rather than producing a test statistic/p-value or interpreting results.
Student must choose the correct conclusion/interpretation from a p-value compared to α — interpreting the result of an inference procedure, matching 4.F.
Student must compute n from SE = σ/√n — a numerical calculation of a sampling distribution parameter, matching 3.D rather than interpreting results or verifying conditions.
The student must select the correct inference procedure from options, not state hypotheses or check conditions—this is identifying an appropriate statistical inference method.
The student must compute the expected value of a discrete random variable—a numerical summary statistic calculation, not an interpretation of meaning or claim.
Student must identify the type of inference error (rejecting a true null), which is naming an error type, not computing or interpreting results.

The student must interpret a confidence interval for slope and draw a conclusion about significance—an interpretation/justification task, not a calculation. The only listed skill code available is 3.B, though the task is interpretive; given the provided list, 3.B is selected.
Student must reason about how α and sample size relate to power—identifying relationships among components of inference (power, Type I/II error), not computing or interpreting a result.

Student must explain/justify why higher confidence yields wider interval—reasoning about the interval's properties and critical value, not computing or checking conditions. Best fit among options is justifying the method/interval reasoning, 4.E.

Student must interpret a p-value from a slope test and state the strongest valid conclusion, including limits on causal claims — this is interpreting/justifying a statistical inference conclusion, not computing a statistic.
The student must select which inference procedure fits two independent samples of proportions—identifying the appropriate method, not stating hypotheses or checking conditions.

The student must interpret a confidence interval for slope in context, drawing a conclusion about the population slope—an interpretation task rather than calculation. Only 3.B is listed, so it is selected by default despite the interpretive nature.

The student computes and describes center, shape, outlier, and effects on summary statistics—describing a distribution's representation and summary statistics rather than justifying a claim with evidence.

The core task is computing z-scores (relative position) for both quizzes, with the comparison and explanation following directly from those calculations. Skill 3.B covers calculating summary statistics and relative positions.

Student must evaluate/justify which statement correctly links random assignment to causal inference—reasoning about appropriate method and conditions for ethically/validly drawing conclusions from design, rather than merely extracting information.

The bulk of the task is computing mean and SD of a binomial distribution (parts b, c), with a probability calc in (d). The dominant cognitive demand is calculating parameters for a probability distribution.

Though part (a) is identification, the bulk of the item requires critiquing bias, describing a proper SRS procedure, and justifying limits on generalization—i.e., justifying appropriate methods for ethically gathering data.

The dominant task is computing the mean and standard deviation of the sampling distribution (parameters of a probability distribution), with CLT justification secondary. Parts a, b, d are calculations of distribution parameters.

The student must recognize and identify each variable's type from given information—no computation, modeling, or interpretation. That matches identifying information to answer a question.
